newsitem.title: MEXICO: Eight die as millions of Mexicans fete Virgin.
newsitem.headline: Eight die as millions of Mexicans fete Virgin.

text.p: At least eight people died and 15 were injured as millions of Roman Catholics flocked to Mexico City on Thursday, some crawling on bloodied knees and others whizzing past on bicycles, to pay their annual tribute to the Virgin of Guadalupe.

A 60-year-old Mexican who had come from his home in the United States, identified as Juan Bautista Galindo, died after suffering a heart attack just three blocks before reaching the vast modern Basilica devoted to the Virgin, police said.

A 12-year-old boy, Miguel Angel Castillo, died when his bicycle was hit by a bus near the shrine, authorities said. Six other pilgrims died in the early hours of Thursday and 15 were injured when their bus collided with a truck on the highway linking the capital to the central city of Puebla.

Authorities said they expected up to 6 million faithful to make the pilgrimage to the Mexico's most venerated shrine, in the north of the capital, between Thursday and Sunday. The Virgin of Guadalupe, a symbol of Mexican nationhood and patron of all Latin America, is said to have appeared several times to a poor Aztec Indian, Juan Diego, in 1531.
The Roman Catholic church says her image was miraculously imprinted on Diego's cloak, which can still be seen at the basilica, set in gold at the centre of the elaborate altar.

The report of the Virgin's appearance so soon after the Spanish Conquest, at a site associated with a pre-Hispanic goddess known as the White Lady, came to symbolise the conversion to Catholicism of Mexico's indigenous population.
Diego was beatified by Pope John Paul II in 1990 during his second trip to Mexico.

Mexican primate Norberto Rivera called on Mexicans on Thursday, a national holiday, to strengthen their faith in the Virgin of Guadalupe despite the crushing economic crisis of 1995, from which the country is still emerging.
"In her name I promise you that if we do so, all our national and personal troubles will fade away," he said.

The vast majority of Mexico's 91 million inhabitants are Roman Catholic and 14 million people visit the basilica every year. "In Mexico even the communists believe in the Virgin of Guadalupe," policeman Agustin Fuentes said on Thursday as he took part in a 3,200-man security operation, "Basilica 96."

Throngs of pilgrims, some on foot, others on bicycles, some singing and dancing and some hobbling on bloodied knees, have been arriving at the basilica, which holds more than 12,000 people at a time, since Wednesday.
"I have come to give thanks to 'Lupita' for giving back my 5-year-old boy's health," said manual worker Alberto Lopez, a father of four, as he advanced painfully on his knees.
Inside, traditional Mariachi bands played the Mexican birthday song "Las Mananitas" in honour of the Virgin's day.
